en: The Parivāra:
The Second Part of the Analysis of the Monks' Rules (Bhikkhuvibhaṅga)
1.6 Section on Combinations (Samuccayavāra) On account of engaging in sexual intercourse, how many offenses does one incur?
On account of engaging in sexual intercourse, one incurs four offenses.
If one engages in sexual intercourse with a body that is completely decayed, it is an offense of defeat (pārājika);
if one engages in sexual intercourse with a body that is mostly decayed, it is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya);
if one inserts the genitals without touching them into a mouth that has been rounded off, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Regarding the offense entailing expiation for using a dildo:
on account of engaging in sexual intercourse, one incurs these four offenses.
To how many of the four failures do those offenses belong?
Of the seven classes of offenses, by how many classes of offenses are they comprised?
Of the six origins of offenses, from how many origins do they originate?
Of the four legal issues, to which legal issue do they belong?
By how many of the seven methods of settling are those offenses settled?
Those offenses fall under two of the four failures:
they may be a failure in virtue, or they may be a failure in conduct.
Of the seven classes of offenses, they are included within four classes of offenses:

they may be included in the class of offenses involving defeat (pārājika), they may be in the class of serious offenses (thullaccaya), they may be in the class of offenses requiring expiation (pācittiya), or they may be in the class of offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Of the six origins of offenses, they originate from one origin.
They originate from both body and mind, not from speech.
Of the four kinds of legal issues, it is the issue arising from an offense.
Of the seven principles for settling disputes, it is settled by three of those principles.
There may be [cases settled] by resolution face-to-face (*sammukhāvinaya*) and by acting according to what has been admitted (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*);

there may be [cases settled] by resolution face-to-face and by covering over as with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*) … [as before] … How many offenses does one commit by reason of performing defecation, urination, or spitting in water out of disrespect?
By reason of performing defecation, urination, or spitting in water out of disrespect, one commits one offense.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa):
by reason of acting out of disrespect, through the act of voiding feces, urine, or spittle in water, one incurs this one offense.
To how many of the four failures does that offense belong?
Of the seven classes of offenses, by how many classes of offenses are they comprised?
Of the six origins of offenses, from how many origins do they originate?
Of the four legal issues, which legal issue is it?
By how many of the seven methods of settling is that offense settled?
That offense belongs to one of the four failures— namely,
failure in conduct.
It is included within one of the seven classes of offenses—
the class of offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
It originates from one of the six origins of offenses.
It originates from both body and mind, not from speech.
Of the four kinds of legal issues, it is an issue arising from an offense.
Among the seven principles for settling disputes, it is settled by three of those principles.
It may be by means of both *sammukhāvinaya* and *paṭiññātakaraṇa*; it may be by means of both *sammukhāvinaya* and *tiṇavatthāraka*.
The eighth section on combinations is finished.
The eight sections on conditions are finished.
The sixteen great sections in the Mahāvibhaṅga are concluded.
The Great Section on the Analysis of the Monks' Rules is finished.
